title: Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan
description: An illustrated map of Mysore under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan, from a soldier’s rise at Devanahalli and Dindigul through the conquests of Bednur, Malabar and Chitradurga and four wars with the East India Company, to Pollilur, the envoys to Versailles, the rockets, the storming of Srirangapatna in 1799 and Tipu’s Tiger.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of Mysore under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan, 1720 to 1799
note: Based on Company records and British and French memoirs, Mysore court histories in Persian, Tipu’s own letters, and Kannada and Malayalam tradition; each chapter says which it follows. Many figures, especially for deportations and conversions, are disputed estimates, and how Tipu is remembered is still argued over. The map is stylised and not to scale; the areas under Powers are painted loosely and are not borders.

steps.title: A soldier’s son
steps.text: Hyder Ali was born about 1720, probably at Budikote, near Kolar, where his father, Fath Muhammad, commanded a small fort. His father died in battle when Hyder was a boy, and he grew up a soldier. He never learned to read or write, yet he rose by his skill with horses, men and money.
steps.today: Today: Budikote, Kolar district, Karnataka.

steps.title: The siege of Devanahalli
steps.text: Mysore was ruled by the Wodeyar kings, but real power lay with two brothers, the general Devaraja and the minister Nanjaraja. In 1749 their army besieged the fort of Devanahalli, and Hyder, serving under his elder brother, was noticed for his daring. Devanahalli fell, and in November 1750 Hyder’s son Tipu was born there.
steps.today: Today: Devanahalli fort, north of Bengaluru, with a memorial at Tipu’s birthplace.

steps.title: The arsenal at Dindigul
steps.text: In 1755 Hyder was made military governor (faujdar) of Dindigul, a fortress on Mysore’s southern frontier. With the help of French gunners and engineers he set up an arsenal there and trained his troops in European drill and artillery. The post gave him an army and revenues of his own, the base for everything that followed.
steps.today: Today: the rock fort at Dindigul, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Master of Mysore
steps.text: In 1760 the minister Khande Rao, with backing from the palace and help from a Maratha army, turned on Hyder, and Hyder fled Srirangapatna. Within a year he was back, defeated Khande Rao and took control. He kept the Wodeyar king, Krishnaraja II, on the throne in name, but from 1761 Hyder ruled Mysore.
steps.today: Today: Srirangapatna, an island town on the Kaveri, Mandya district, Karnataka.

steps.title: The treasure of Bednur
steps.text: In 1763 Hyder marched north-west against Bednur, capital of the Keladi Nayakas, who held the hills and the coast of Kanara. He took the city and, by most accounts, a vast treasure, which paid for his army. He renamed it Haidarnagar and planned it as a second capital. The Kanara ports gave Mysore the sea.
steps.today: Today: Nagara, the old Bednur, Shivamogga district, Karnataka.

steps.title: The Zamorin’s fire
steps.text: In 1766 Hyder marched down the coast into Malabar. The Zamorin, the Hindu king of Calicut, whose predecessors had received Vasco da Gama, could not stop him. Rather than surrender, most accounts say, the Zamorin set fire to his palace and died in it. Hyder took Malabar, but Nair revolts against Mysore rule went on for years.
steps.today: Today: Kozhikode, Kerala.

steps.title: At the gates of Madras
steps.text: In 1767 the first war with the Company began. After defeats in the open field, Hyder changed tactics. In March 1769 he rode with his cavalry to within a few miles of Madras, and the council at Fort St George signed a treaty: conquests were returned, and each side promised to help the other if attacked.
steps.today: Today: Fort St George, Chennai, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Obavva’s pestle
steps.text: Hyder besieged Chitradurga, the hill fort of the Nayakas, more than once. Tradition tells that a guard’s wife, Obavva, found his soldiers creeping through a gap in the rocks and struck them down one by one with a rice pestle (onake). The gap is still shown. In 1779 Hyder took the fort, and its last Nayaka died his prisoner.
steps.today: Today: Chitradurga fort, with Onake Obavva’s gap (Obavvana Kindi).

steps.title: Pollilur
steps.text: In July 1780 Hyder poured into the Carnatic with a huge army, starting the second war. On 10 September, near Pollilur, his forces and Tipu’s surrounded a Company column under Colonel William Baillie. Mysore rockets set off its ammunition carts. Most of the column was killed or captured, and Baillie died a prisoner. It was among the Company’s worst defeats.
steps.today: Today: Pullalur, near Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Porto Novo
steps.text: The Company sent Sir Eyre Coote, a veteran of its wars against the French, to Madras. On 1 July 1781, at Porto Novo on the coast, his smaller army beat Hyder in a long day’s fighting, and he won again at Pollilur and Sholinghur. Neither side could finish the other, and the war dragged on.
steps.today: Today: Parangipettai, Cuddalore district, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Death in camp
steps.text: Hyder Ali died in his camp near Chittoor on 7 December 1782, probably of a cancer or abscess on his back. His ministers kept the death secret and held the army together until Tipu, then fighting on the west coast, could ride back and take command. Hyder was later laid to rest at Srirangapatna, in a tomb Tipu built.
steps.today: Today: Chittoor, Andhra Pradesh.

steps.title: Peace at Mangalore
steps.text: Tipu won back Bednur from a Company army in 1783 and captured its general, Richard Mathews, who died in captivity. He then besieged the Company’s garrison at Mangalore for most of a year until it surrendered. In March 1784 the Treaty of Mangalore ended the war: each side returned its conquests and released its prisoners.
steps.today: Today: Mangaluru, Dakshina Kannada, Karnataka.

steps.title: The Sultan’s court
steps.text: Tipu took the title of emperor (padshah) in 1786. He issued new coins, began a new calendar, renamed months and towns and reorganised weights, measures and trade. In 1784 he built a summer palace, the Daria Daulat Bagh, on the island of Srirangapatna, and had its walls painted with scenes, among them the victory at Pollilur.
steps.today: Today: the Daria Daulat Bagh, Srirangapatna, now a museum.

steps.title: Envoys to Versailles
steps.text: Tipu looked abroad for allies. One embassy went to the Ottoman sultan at Constantinople. Another sailed from Pondicherry in 1787, and in August 1788 its three envoys were received by King Louis XVI at Versailles. They were feted, and one was painted by Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, but France, nearing revolution, promised no alliance.
steps.today: Today: Puducherry, once the capital of French India.

steps.title: A harsher record
steps.text: Tipu’s rule had a harsher side. After revolts in Kodagu and Malabar his armies deported thousands, and accounts, among them his own letters, record forced conversions to Islam. In 1784 he deported the Catholics of the Kanara coast to Srirangapatna; their number, put at 30,000 to 80,000, is disputed. Historians still argue whether his motives were religious or political.
steps.today: Today: Madikeri fort, Kodagu district, Karnataka.

steps.title: The fall of Bangalore
steps.text: In 1789 Tipu attacked the lines of Travancore, a Company ally, and the third war began. The Governor-General, Lord Cornwallis, took command himself, allied with the Marathas and the Nizam. His army marched up from the Carnatic and stormed Bangalore’s fort on 21 March 1791. Nearby, the Lalbagh garden, begun by Hyder and finished by Tipu, survives.
steps.today: Today: Bangalore fort and Tipu Sultan’s summer palace, Bengaluru.

steps.title: Letters to Sringeri
steps.text: In 1791 a Maratha army under the Patwardhans raided the monastery (matha) at Sringeri, killing and plundering and disturbing the image of the goddess Sharada. Tipu wrote to its head, the Shankaracharya, condemning the raid, and sent money and grain to reconsecrate the goddess. About thirty of his letters to Sringeri were found in 1916.
steps.today: Today: the Sringeri Sharada Peetham, Chikkamagaluru district, Karnataka.

steps.title: Hostage princes
steps.text: Cornwallis besieged Srirangapatna in February 1792, and Tipu sued for peace. By the Treaty of Seringapatam he gave up half his kingdom to the Company, the Marathas and the Nizam, and agreed to pay a huge indemnity. Until it was paid, two of his young sons were held as hostages. British artists painted the handover; the boys returned in 1794.
steps.today: Today: Srirangapatna, Mandya district, Karnataka.

steps.title: Citizen Tipu
steps.text: Tipu still hoped for France. In 1798 the governor of Mauritius, then French, issued a proclamation calling for volunteers to serve him, and about a hundred landed at Mangalore. British accounts say a Jacobin club met at Srirangapatna and called him Citizen Tipu. To the new Governor-General, Richard Wellesley, it was proof of a French alliance.
steps.today: Today: Mangaluru; Mauritius lies about 4,000 km to the south-west.

steps.title: Rockets in a well
steps.text: Mysore’s armies used rockets: iron tubes packed with powder and lashed to bamboo poles or blades, fired in volleys by trained rocket men. Captured rockets were studied in Britain, and William Congreve built on them for the rockets he developed from 1804. Excavations at Nagara, the old Bednur, from 2017 found hundreds of unused rockets in a disused well.
steps.today: Today: Nagara fort, Shivamogga district; Mysore rockets are also held in British collections.

steps.title: The storming of Srirangapatna
steps.text: In 1799 Wellesley sent two armies against Tipu, one from Vellore and one from the west coast, with the Nizam’s troops. They besieged Srirangapatna, and on 4 May, at about one in the afternoon, the storming parties under General David Baird crossed the river into a breach. Tipu fought at the walls and was killed near the Water Gate.
steps.today: Today: the breach and the spot where Tipu’s body was found are marked at Srirangapatna.

steps.title: The Wodeyars restored
steps.text: Tipu was buried in the Gumbaz beside his father. The Company took the coast and much of the land around, and gave the rest back to the Wodeyars as a smaller Mysore under its protection. Krishnaraja Wodeyar III, aged five, was crowned at Mysore, with Purnaiah, once Tipu’s finance minister, as his chief minister (dewan).
steps.today: Today: the Mysore Palace, Mysuru, rebuilt in 1912.

steps.title: Tipu’s Tiger
steps.text: The palace was looted. Among the spoils was a life-size wooden tiger mauling a European soldier; turn a handle and it growls while the man cries out. The tiger was Tipu’s emblem. Shipped to London, it is now in the Victoria and Albert Museum. In India, Tipu is still remembered both as a hero of resistance and as a tyrant.
steps.today: Today: Tipu’s Tiger, Victoria and Albert Museum, London; the Gumbaz, Srirangapatna.

rulers.text: Krishnaraja II, with Devaraja and Nanjaraja

items.name: Hyder Ali
items.text: A soldier who could not read, Hyder rose through the Mysore army to rule the kingdom from 1761, keeping the Wodeyar kings as figureheads. He took Bednur, Malabar and Chitradurga, used French help to modernise his army, and twice fought the East India Company. He died in camp in 1782, during the second war.

items.name: Tipu Sultan
items.text: Hyder’s eldest son, born at Devanahalli, he fought beside his father and ruled Mysore from 1782. He reformed coins, calendar and trade, sought allies in France and the Ottoman empire, and used rockets against the Company. His rule was harsh to rebels and to some religious communities. He died defending Srirangapatna in 1799.

items.name: Krishnaraja Wodeyar II
items.text: Placed on the throne as a child, he reigned while the brothers Devaraja and Nanjaraja held real power, and then Hyder Ali. After 1761 he was king in name only. Hyder kept the Wodeyar family on the throne after his death, and in 1799 the Company restored the family to power under its protection.

items.name: Obavva
items.text: Known as Onake Obavva, Obavva of the pestle. Tradition says she was the wife of a guard at Chitradurga and, finding Hyder’s soldiers creeping in through a gap in the rocks, killed them one by one with a pestle. Her story is a favourite of Karnataka’s folk tradition and is taught in its schools.

items.name: Eyre Coote
items.text: An Irish-born general who had beaten the French at Wandiwash in 1760, Coote returned to India as commander-in-chief. Old and ill, he still beat Hyder at Porto Novo and in other battles of 1781. He died at Madras in 1783, soon after landing for another campaign.

items.name: Purnaiah
items.text: A Brahmin accountant from a poor family, Purnaiah served Hyder and became Tipu’s chief finance minister. When Hyder died, he helped keep the news secret until Tipu arrived. After 1799 the Company made him dewan of the restored Mysore, which he ran for the young Krishnaraja III until 1811.

items.name: Lord Cornwallis
items.text: Remembered in Britain for surrendering at Yorktown in 1781, Charles Cornwallis became Governor-General in 1786. In the third war he led the army himself, took Bangalore and besieged Srirangapatna, forcing Tipu to give up half his kingdom in 1792. He returned to India in 1805 and died there that year.

items.name: Richard Wellesley
items.text: Governor-General from 1798, he saw Tipu’s dealings with France as a threat and launched the fourth war in 1799. His younger brother Arthur, the future Duke of Wellington, served in the campaign and became governor of Srirangapatna afterwards. Wellesley pressed Indian rulers into alliances that put them under Company control.
